points.description: Child is created/ready in kernel mode and has no trap of its own, so it needs a prepared kernel context (saved context/kernel stack) set up by fork so it can be scheduled and run in kernel mode.
points.partial_credit: Mentions the child runs in kernel mode or needs a context, but vaguely.

points.description: The child's context is set up so that, when first scheduled, it starts executing at a specific function (e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack is arranged so that function's return address is the trap-return code (e.g., trapret).
points.partial_credit: Only one of the two: starts at a function, or return address on the stack set to trap return.

points.description: Result: the child returns from that function into the trap return path, emulating a call to and return from the trap handler, and then unwinds the rest of the kernel stack (trap frame) to return to user space.
points.partial_credit: Says it returns to user mode via trap return but does not explain the emulation or stack unrolling.

rubric.notes: Full marks (2) need the key idea: fork sets up the child's kernel context/stack so that on first scheduling it runs a function (like forkret) that returns to the trap-return code, faking a return from a trap, then unwinds to user mode. Part marks for stating only some of this, or stating it vaguely (e.g., 'it returns like the parent' with no stack/return address setup). Give nothing for answers that say the child actually takes a trap or that give no kernel stack/return mechanism.
